title: The dish just out of reach
hookLine: small bits of effort shape behavior more than willpower
carry: friction shapes us more than willpower

lines: A DISH, A LITTLE FARTHER BACK.
cards: A cafeteria line, lunchtime, trays sliding along a rail. Researchers quietly move one dish a little farther back, just beyond easy reach. Nobody hides it.
Nobody makes a rule. Anyone who wants it only has to lean in. And people take less of it.
Not because they made a resolution, or summoned some inner strength. Because of a lean.

Habit researchers draw a strange lesson from studies like this one: the tiniest bit of extra effort, a step, a reach, a second click, can move behavior more than all the willpower anyone brought to lunch.

teach.b: First, the reach. In cafeteria studies, researchers led by Paul Rozin found that making a food slightly harder to get to, a little farther away, reduced how much of it people took.
A small change in distance, a real change in behavior.
Second, friction beats will, or so habit researchers argue. Psychologists who study habit, Wendy Wood among them, call these small costs friction.
Willpower is what people tend to reach for first, and it can be unreliable. Friction works quietly, without asking anyone to try harder.
Third, add friction to what you'd rather do less: the phone charging in another room, the snacks on a high shelf.

teach.h: A SMALL HILL FOR WHAT YOU WANT LESS.
teach.b: Not a ban, just a small hill to climb, and small hills turn out to matter.
Fourth, take friction away from what you want to do more: the running shoes by the door, the cushion already on the floor, the book on the pillow instead of the shelf.
William James, in his chapter on habit, wrote: "The great thing, then, in all education, is to make our nervous system our ally instead of our enemy."

Friction is one of the plainest ways to do that: rearrange the room so the easy thing and the good thing are the same thing. A practice that needs a heroic effort to begin may not survive a busy week.
A practice that's one step away has a fighting chance.

how: People building a habit sometimes arrange their surroundings so the practice takes as few steps as possible, leaving out what they need the night before, and put small obstacles in the way of habits they want to do less.

o: removing every rule so you do what you like
pushing through resistance with more willpower
making a good habit one small step easier to start

games.q: friction, both ways: tap the pairs.
p: a dish a little farther away
a small hill for what you want less
make the nervous system an ally

s: in the cafeteria studies, people took less only when the food was hidden
nothing was hidden. it was just slightly harder to reach.
friction works without asking anyone to try harder

games.q: you keep meaning to meditate in the morning, but the cushion is in the closet behind the vacuum. what do you do?
o: leave the cushion out on the floor tonight.
decide meditation just isn't for you.
games.why: take one step of friction away. habit researchers argue small effort changes move behavior more than willpower does.

practice: Settle on the breath, then walk through tomorrow's practice step by step, the way it actually happens, and find the one step that most often stops you.
Picture removing it, the cushion left out, the app moved to the first screen, the alarm set the night before, and choose just one. Then let the planning go and rest on the breath.

wordCard.voice: Less friction. Small bits of effort shape what people do more than willpower, so make the good thing one step easier. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: friction shapes us more than willpower. A small hill can matter more than a big push. Until tomorrow.
